A classifier is trained on landscapes with a particular geometry and then applied
to new ones. When the application landscapes differ from the training data, the
two workflows behave differently, and some of these differences can affect
predictions. This guide explains which differences matter, what the package
checks, and what you need to check or prepare.

You can use this guide after converting raster or matrix data to `landscape`
objects as described in
[Import user-defined landscapes](importing-landscapes.html). Check the landscape
geometry before training or applying a classifier with the
[metric-based](classify-metrics.html) or
[pixel-based](classify-pixels.html) workflow.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(patternscaper)
```

## Landscape geometry

When comparing training and application landscapes, consider:

| Property | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Extent** | width and height of the area covered | train on 100 × 100 cells, apply to 200 × 200 cells at the same resolution |
| **Resolution** | ground size represented by one cell | train on 1 m cells, apply to 30 m cells |
| **Aspect ratio** | ratio of columns to rows | train on 100 × 100 cells, apply to 200 × 80 cells |
| **Shape** | rectangular or irregular study-area outline | apply to a clipped catchment boundary |

A raster grid is rectangular. An irregular study area is therefore usually
represented by `NA` cells outside its boundary. Landscapes generated with
`create_landscape()` or `create_landscapes()` are complete rectangles without
such a mask.

## Metric-based workflow

`calculate_metrics()` records the geometry of each landscape, and `train_metric_model()` stores a summary of this recorded training geometry in the model. When you later call `apply_metric_model()`, it compares the application landscapes against that summary and warns when:

- the width or height of the extent differs by more than 25%
- cell resolution differs by more than 1%
- aspect ratio differs by more than 25%

These warnings hint at potential problems but do not determine whether a
prediction is reliable. If a model was trained from a manually created metrics
table without geometry columns, these checks are skipped and the function reports
this.

Whether a mismatch affects predictions also depends on which metrics the model
uses. Raw area and count metrics, and some shape metrics, can change strongly with
spatial extent. Density metrics and normalized composition or configuration
metrics can be less sensitive. However, no metric is guaranteed to be robust to
changes in geometry.

Because `evaluate_metrics()` ranks metrics by their ability to distinguish
patterns and does not assess robustness to geometry, calculate the selected
metrics for labelled landscapes with the expected extents, resolutions, and
shapes. Compare their values within each pattern class and evaluate the fitted
model on these landscapes before applying it to unlabelled data.

The same concern also applies to the training data. `train_metric_model()` warns when training dimensions or resolution vary between landscapes, because scale-dependent metrics may then conflate the pattern with the landscape geometry.

## Pixel-based workflow

The CNN has fixed input dimensions. When an application raster has a different number of rows or columns, `apply_pixel_model()` resamples it to the training
dimensions using nearest-neighbour resampling. The CNN only looks at the cell array, not the spatial extent or resolution of the raster. The package therefore does not
check whether training and application data represent comparable ecological scales.

The automatic resizing of application landscapes does not make the CNN independent of scale. Predictions can still change when resizing changes the size or shape of the landscape structures. Before resizing, `apply_pixel_model()` performs two geometry-related checks:

1. **Aspect ratio**: If the ratio of columns to rows differs from the training grid by more than 10%, resizing stretches the raster anisotropically and `apply_pixel_model()` warns about this.
2. **`NA` cells**: They cannot be interpreted as a land-cover category. Therefore, the function raises an error and you have to correct the landscapes.

For training, the pixel workflow requires one categorical raster layer per landscape, identical numbers of rows and columns in all landscapes, and no `NA` cells. Otherwise the function raises an error. However, it does not check whether otherwise matching training rasters have the same spatial resolution.

Land-cover categories must be numeric whole-number codes. Training fixes one input
channel for each code. An application raster may omit a trained code but cannot
introduce a code not seen during training.

Both workflows require each code to represent the same land-cover type in both training and application data.

## Prepare application data

### Match the resolution

Landscapes generated by `patternscaper` have dimensionless resolution 1. Decide
what one cell represents and use a comparable ecological grain in the training
and application data. For metric models, raster resolution must also use
comparable spatial units.

If categorical rasters must be resampled, use a method appropriate for
categorical data, such as nearest-neighbour resampling. Upsampling does not add
spatial detail.

### Handle missing cells

Metric models can be applied to irregular areas represented by `NA`, but the
package does not compare the shapes of the missing-cell masks. Test the model on
labelled landscapes with similar outlines.

Pixel models reject `NA`. If missing cells lie outside the study boundary, crop
an `NA`-free rectangle with the training aspect ratio or divide the area into
complete windows. Small gaps inside the study area may instead be imputed, for
example with nearest-neighbour filling for categorical data. Do not fill cells
outside the study boundary with a land-cover code.
